function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **ready‑to‑run recipe** that you can paste into a terminal (or copy into a shell script) and run against the `nodejs-welcome` repo.  
It will:

1. Clone the repo.  
2. Create a Dockerfile, a Kubernetes deployment/service YAML, and a GitHub Actions workflow that builds the image on every push to `main`.  
3. Stage, commit, and push the new files back to the repo.

> **NOTE** – The helper functions you saw in the “Tools” section are only for Python projects.  
> For a Node.js repo we’ll hand‑craft the files instead.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# If you already have a clone, skip this step
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create the artefacts

> *We’re assuming the repo contains a simple Express app that listens on port 3000 and has a `package.json` with a start script (`node app.js`).*  
> If your repo differs, tweak the files below accordingly.

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the repo root:

```dockerfile
# Use the official lightweight Node.js image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is small, fast, and stable.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees a reproducible install.  
> * The `EXPOSE` line documents the port for Kubernetes and Docker Compose users.

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a file named `k8s-nodejs-welcome.yaml` in the repo root:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: node:18-alpine   # Replace with your own image registry if you push to Docker Hub/GCR
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **What this does**  
> * Deploys two replicas of the app.  
> * Exposes the service internally on port 80, forwarding to the container’s port 3000.  
> * You can change `type: ClusterIP` to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` if you need external access.

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create the directory `.github/workflows` if it doesn’t exist, then add a file named `build-and-push.yml`:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout source
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: Dockerfile
        push: true
        tags: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **How to use this workflow**  
> 1. Create a Docker Hub account (or use GitHub Container Registry).  
> 2. In the repo’s Settings → Secrets → Actions, add:
>    * `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub username.  
>    * `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` – a Docker Hub access token (or password).  
> 3. Commit the workflow file.  
> 4. On every push to `main`, the action will build the image and push it to Docker Hub.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage the new files

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s-nodejs-welcome.yaml .github/workflows/build-and-push.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes YAML, and GitHub Actions workflow"
git push origin main
```

---

## 🎉 Done!

You now have:

- A production‑ready Dockerfile for your Node.js app.  
- A Kubernetes deployment/service YAML that you can apply with `kubectl apply -f k8s-nodejs-welcome.yaml`.  
- A CI workflow that automatically builds and pushes the Docker image whenever you push to `main`.

Feel free to tweak the image name, tags, or Kubernetes settings to match your deployment strategy. Happy coding!
